China's New Trademark Law Takes Effect 1 January 2027: What Foreign Brands Should Do Now

China's first full rewrite of its Trademark Law since 1983 takes effect on 1 January 2027. Here is what actually changes for foreign brand owners — and what to do in the remaining weeks.

The Short Answer: Keep Filing Early — But Not to "Lock In" the Old Law

On 26 June 2026, China adopted a completely revised Trademark Law. It takes effect on 1 January 2027. This is the first full rewrite since 1983: the statute grows from 8 chapters and 73 articles to 9 chapters and 87 articles, with a new chapter devoted to registrability conditions.

If you own a foreign brand with Chinese trademark rights, or are about to file, the practical answer is: keep filing early, but do not file purely to "lock in" the old rules. Under the CNIPA's draft transition measures published on 28 September 2026, an application filed before 1 January 2027 but decided on or after that date is handled under the new law.

What early filing still buys you is the one thing that has always mattered most in China: the earliest filing date. China remains a first-to-file jurisdiction. The 2027 law changes examination standards, procedural deadlines and enforcement powers — it does not change who wins when two parties claim the same mark.

Status note: The revised law is enacted and its effective date is fixed. The CNIPA's Measures for Handling Business Matters Following the Revised Trademark Law are still a draft (public comment closed 12 November 2026) and may change before the final text is issued. We flag draft-based statements below.

Four Dates That Matter

DateWhat happensWhy it matters to you
26 June 2026NPC Standing Committee adopts the revised Trademark LawThe text is final; the 9-chapter / 87-article structure is fixed
28 September 2026CNIPA publishes draft transition measures and a draft Examination and Review GuidelinesShows how pending cases and new filing types are intended to be handled
12 November 2026Public comment on the draft measures closesFinal measures may differ; re-check before relying on transition detail
1 January 2027Revised Trademark Law (and, if adopted, the transition measures) take effectNew opposition window, new registrable signs, new cancellation powers

Source: CNIPA, Main Contents of the Revision to the PRC Trademark Law (10 July 2026) and the CNIPA notice of 28 September 2026.

What Changes for Foreign Applicants

Change2026 law articlePractical effect
Opposition windowArt. 363 months → 2 months after preliminary publication
Refusal reviewArt. 3715 days to request review; CNIPA decides within 9 months (extendable by 3)
Registrable signsArt. 14Dynamic (motion) marks added alongside words, devices, colours and sounds
Bad-faith / speculative filingsArts. 19, 54Applications with no intent to use that clearly exceed normal business needs are refused; warning plus fine up to RMB 100,000
Misleading useArt. 56Fines up to 5× illegal turnover (or RMB 250,000); CNIPA may revoke the registration if not corrected

Should You Rush to File Before 31 December 2026?

This is the question most brand owners are asking in November 2026. The honest answer has two parts.

No — a pre-2027 filing date does not freeze the old examination rules

The draft transition measures follow a general principle of "substantive issues under the old law, procedural issues under the new law". For registration, opposition, refusal review and other applications filed before 1 January 2027 where CNIPA issues its decision on or after that date, the draft provides that the new law applies. For invalidation or cancellation actions against marks already registered before 2027, procedural questions follow the new law while substantive questions follow the law in force when the mark was registered.

Yes — an earlier filing date still protects you under first-to-file

Priority between competing claimants is decided by who filed first, not by which statute was in force. Filing now still secures your position against a squatter, a distributor or a factory that files tomorrow. The new law's stronger bad-faith provisions are a useful additional remedy, but they are not a substitute for being first.

One date is genuinely decisive: the publication date

Under Article 4 of the draft measures, the length of the opposition window is determined by the publication date, not the filing date: for domestic applications, the date of preliminary publication in the Trademark Gazette; for international registrations designating China, the WIPO publication date. Applications published before 1 January 2027 keep the 3-month window; those published on or after that date get 2 months. A window that straddles the year boundary is not restarted. This is the single most operationally important transition rule for any brand running a watch service.

Do not rely on the draft as final. The measures were still open for comment until 12 November 2026. Confirm the final text before setting internal deadlines or advising a client on a live opposition.

Five Things to Do Before 1 January 2027

  1. Audit your portfolio for "no intent to use" exposure. Article 19 refuses applications that lack intent to use and clearly exceed normal business needs. Broad defensive portfolios remain permissible in principle, but every class should have a documented business rationale, expansion plan, anti-counterfeit purpose or sub-class logic behind it.
  2. Upgrade your watch service to a 2-month response cycle. A monthly gazette review plus slow internal approval is no longer safe. Move to weekly monitoring of your key classes and Chinese-character variants, pre-authorise local counsel, and keep an evidence package ready so an opposition can be filed within days of publication. See our monitoring guide.
  3. Build a use-evidence file now. Because CNIPA can cancel idle marks on its own initiative, dated invoices, platform listings with capture dates, packaging, customs records, distributor agreements and exhibition materials should be archived by mark and by class from day one.
  4. Check your Chinese-character coverage. English and Chinese marks are separate rights in China. Confirm that your official Chinese name, common transliterations and consumer-coined nicknames are registered in the classes that matter. Our classification guide explains how sub-classes affect scope.
  5. Re-vet your agent. Articles 65–68 require agencies and their practitioners to be recorded with CNIPA and add penalties for conflicts of interest and knowingly assisting bad-faith filings. Ask your agent for its recordal status and who is personally signing your filings.

What Does Not Change

  • First-to-file. China does not award rights to the first user. A foreign registration has no effect in China.
  • Territorial scope. A CNIPA registration covers mainland China. Separate filings are needed for Hong Kong, China; Macao, China; and Taiwan, China.
  • The local-agent requirement. Foreign applicants without a domicile or place of business in China still file through a Chinese trademark agency.
  • 10-year terms and renewals. Registrations remain valid for 10 years and are renewable; see our renewal guide.
  • The Madrid route. You can still designate China through WIPO, though CNIPA examines under Chinese law. Compare both paths in Madrid vs direct filing.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will my pending application be examined under the old law?

Under the September 2026 draft, if CNIPA decides the case on or after 1 January 2027, the new law generally applies to a pre-2027 application. Treat this as the planning assumption, then confirm against the final measures.

Can I still oppose a mark published in December 2026?

Under the draft, a mark published before 1 January 2027 keeps the 3-month opposition window and the clock is not restarted by the new law. Do not, however, wait until the last week — evidence preparation and translation take time.

Does the new law remove squatters automatically?

No. The bad-faith provisions, the active cancellation power and the wider well-known mark protection are stronger tools, but they are invoked in proceedings. Monitoring and early filing remain the cheapest protection. If a squatter already holds a registration, see your four recovery options.

Sources and Caveats

Primary sources: the full text of the Trademark Law of the PRC (2026 Revision) published by CNIPA (26 June 2026); CNIPA's Main Contents of the Revision (10 July 2026); and the CNIPA notice of 28 September 2026 on the draft transition measures and draft Examination and Review Guidelines. Article numbers in this article refer to the 2026 law. This article is general information, not legal advice; outcomes depend on the specific facts and on the final implementing rules.
